Saturday, home.
Came home for two days. Mummy had kept my room exactly as I left it three years ago: the blue bedsheet, my school trophies dusted, even my old hair clips in the drawer. My sister Sonali whispered that Mummy airs the room every Sunday and sits in there with her tea. Tonight I found Mummy in the hallway, stopped in front of my graduation photo, just looking. She didn't hear me. When she turned round, she smiled like nothing had happened and asked if I wanted more rice.
I've been calling every other week. Short calls. 'All fine, Mummy, busy.' I think those calls are her whole Sunday.
Calling on Wednesdays too from now on. Maybe video.
— Mehak

qa.a: Every Sunday.

qa.q: What might Mummy be feeling as she stands in front of the graduation photo?
qa.a: Mummy seems to be missing Mehak deeply, quietly waiting for a child who has grown up and moved away.

qa.a: Mehak decides to call on Wednesdays too, maybe by video, since even short calls clearly mean a great deal to Mummy.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel about the extra Wednesday calls?
qa.a: Mummy would probably feel less alone in the waiting, and the calls might mean far more to her than the few words spoken. 🤍

passage: In the village near Mandi, the apple blossom was out, and Amma had been cleaning Himani's corner of the room since morning. Himani hadn't lived there for four years, not since the nursing job in Muscat. Sarita, home from her own job in Shimla, watched Amma fold Himani's old shawl, unfold it, fold it again. At dinner Amma glanced at the door twice when the dog barked. Then the phone rang: Himani, a video call, the screen shaky. Amma didn't say much. 'Eating properly? Wearing warm clothes?' But she held the phone with both hands, close to her face, long after the talk had turned to nothing. When it ended, she sat in the dark a while. Sarita put a hand on her shoulder and said nothing.

Paulo flew from Wellington to his mother's house in Hamilton for the long weekend. The first thing he noticed was the kitchen calendar: his arrival circled in red, the circle drawn so many times the paper had gone thin.
His bed was made with the dinosaur duvet he had outgrown at eleven. In the fridge sat three tubs of the seaweed soup his mother, Soo-ah, knew he liked, far more than one person could eat in three days.
On Saturday night he came downstairs for water and found his mother in the hallway, standing in front of his graduation photo. She wasn't doing anything. She was just looking, one finger resting on the frame. She turned, startled, and said, "Oh, you're up. Want tea?"
They drank it without talking much. On Monday, at the airport, she hugged him a beat longer than usual and said, "Call on Sundays. Even two minutes."

qa.q: What was drawn on the kitchen calendar?
qa.a: His arrival was circled in red, drawn so many times the paper had gone thin.

qa.q: What might Soo-ah have been feeling as she stood looking at the graduation photo?
qa.a: She was probably missing Paulo in the everyday way she can no longer have him, and her startled offer of tea suggests she did not want him to see how much she waits.

qa.q: What small choice could Paulo make after this weekend that would matter to his mother?
qa.a: He could keep the Sunday calls, even short ones, since the weekend shows that for Soo-ah a two-minute call carries far more than its words.

qa.q: How does the weekend look from Soo-ah's side?
qa.a: For Soo-ah the days are full of preparing and then quietly holding on, with the red circle, the extra soup and the longer hug all showing a love that now mostly waits.

grounding: It shows a young adult noticing his parent's yearning through the circled calendar, the ready room and the pause at a photograph, where love has become waiting.

Jagdish had never been inside his father's bank in Kanpur, not since he was a small boy. Now twenty-four and home from Hyderabad for Holi, he went to drop off the tiffin Papa had forgotten.
Papa was at the cash counter, so the clerk at the next desk, Preeti ma'am, waved him to a chair. "You're Jagdish! Sit, sit." She tapped the glass on Papa's desk. Under it was a photo Jagdish had forgotten existed: him at the Class 10 prize day, all teeth. "He shows everyone," she said. "And at lunch he checks his phone, puts it down, checks again. We tease him that he is waiting for a call from the prime minister."
Jagdish looked at the photo, then at his father counting notes, head bent, grey at the temples. He had called maybe twice a month since January. When Papa finally came over, Jagdish said only, "Tiffin," and held it out, but his voice came out rough.

qa.a: It was under the glass on Papa's desk.

qa.q: Why does Jagdish's voice come out rough when he hands over the tiffin?
qa.a: Preeti ma'am's words and the old photo have shown him how much his father waits for him, and he is moved and perhaps a little guilty about calling only twice a month.

qa.q: What could Jagdish choose to do differently once he is back in Hyderabad?
qa.a: He could call his father more often, even briefly at lunchtime, now that he knows Papa checks his phone again and again hoping to hear from him.

qa.q: How does Preeti ma'am see Jagdish's father?
qa.a: She sees a colleague who is proud of his son and quietly lonely for him, and she teases him kindly about the phone while making sure Jagdish learns about it.

grounding: It shows a young adult discovering his father's longing through a photo kept at work and a phone checked for calls, so a simple call now means more than words.

Dear Sangeeta Didi,
I was home last week while you were in Chennai. I have to tell you something small.
On the first evening, I went into my old room. Papa had changed the bedsheet, the one with blue checks I liked, and put a new bulb in my study lamp. Nobody sleeps in there anymore.
Later I saw him in the hall, standing in front of the photo from my graduation. Not doing anything. Just standing, his hand on the frame.
When I asked if he was okay, he said, "Dust," and walked off. Didi, it wasn't dust.
I've been calling home once a week. I'm going to call every other day now, even for two minutes. I think those two minutes carry more than we think.
Farhan

qa.a: He changed the bedsheet to the blue checked one and put a new bulb in the study lamp.

Damini, you asked what surprised me most about going home. I'm Charu, and it's this.
I'd been in Hyderabad two years. Went home to Indore for Diwali. My room was exactly as I left it. Same posters, same pens in the same cup. Maa had dusted everything. The mattress had a fresh sheet as if I'd be sleeping there every night.
On the last morning, I came down early and saw her at the kitchen window, holding the phone with my photo on the screen. Just looking. She didn't see me.
I went back upstairs and sat on the bed for a while.
Now I call her on my walk to work. Ten minutes. I don't have much news. She doesn't either. But she always sounds different by the end, lighter.
I didn't know love could look like waiting.

I'm Gurpreet. My brother Arnab and I both went home to Ludhiana in March, first time together in a year. This is what I noticed.
Mum had made the rajma on the first night, the one we fought over as kids. She kept putting more on our plates.
Every evening she found a reason to come into our old rooms. To bring a towel. To fix a curtain. To ask nothing in particular.
On our last night, Arnab went to get water and I heard him stop in the hallway. Mum was standing at the photo wall, touching the one of us on the scooter. Arnab didn't say anything. He just stood next to her.
When we left, she waved from the gate until the auto turned the corner. Arnab said quietly, "We should come more." I nodded. I think we both understood what the rajma had been saying.

qa.q: What was Mum touching on the photo wall?
qa.a: The photo of the two of them on the scooter.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling when Arnab said "We should come more"?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt moved and a bit guilty, understanding the love behind Mum's waiting.

qa.q: What could Gurpreet and Arnab do after this visit?
qa.a: They could visit more often and call regularly, since small contact means a lot to a parent who is waiting.

qa.q: How might Mum have felt waving from the gate?
qa.a: She probably felt a mix of love and sadness, wanting them to stay longer and already missing them.

grounding: It shows a young adult observing a parent's yearning in cooking, visits to their rooms and a photograph.

"Sabina, you asked why I call my mother every day at seven. Let me tell you something from when I was about your age.
I had moved to Chennai for my first job. When I went back to Madurai for Pongal, my room was exactly as I had left it, my old hair clips still on the shelf. I laughed at her. I said, 'Amma, rent it out.' She only said, 'It's your room, beti.'
That night I woke for water and saw her standing at my door, just looking at me sleeping. In the morning she was busy and cheerful again.
I, Leela, understood then that she had been waiting in that room for two years. After that, my calls were never short. Five minutes to me was the best part of her evening."

qa.a: Seeing Amma silently watching her sleep; it showed her that a short call meant a great deal, so she stopped keeping calls short.

qa.a: She probably felt hurt and unseen, because the room was how she kept her daughter close while waiting.

The power was out across the whole block when Manoj reached home late on Friday, his flight delayed by rain. His friend Arnab had driven him from the airport and came up to help with the bag.
By the light of a phone torch they found the dining table set for one, the food covered with plates and gone cold. Manoj's father was asleep in the chair beside it, still in his shirt, an old album open on his lap at a photo of Manoj's first day at college.
Arnab whispered, "He waited for you."
Manoj stood very still. His father had said on the phone, "No need to hurry." He woke him gently. His father's first words were, "Eat something," and then, softer, "You're thin."
Manoj ate the cold food by torchlight and did not mention the delay.

'Baba, why is my bicycle still in the balcony?'
Bidisha's father looked up from the paper. 'Where else would it go?'
'I left for Bengaluru two years ago.'
'You might come back one day and want to ride.'
Pranav, Bidisha's husband, caught her eye.
'And the mosquito net on my old bed?'
'It's monsoon. You never know.'
'Baba, I visit twice a year.'
Her father folded the newspaper slowly. 'Your mother puts out your plate every Sunday. Out of habit.' He looked at the door. 'We wait. It's what parents do.'
Bidisha's eyes filled. She sat beside him. 'I'll come for Durga Puja, Baba. And I'll call on Sundays when Ma puts out the plate.'
Her father patted her hand and didn't say anything for a while.

passage: I went home to Aizawl in December for the first time since starting work in Delhi. My mother, Lalremsiami, had kept my room exactly as it was. Same quilt, same books, same school certificate on the wall. My sister Ira whispered, 'Nu sits in here some evenings. She doesn't say anything.' On my third evening, I saw it myself. My mother stood at the door of my room, holding a cup of tea, just looking at my bed. She didn't know I was in the corridor. I understood then that for her, loving me now mostly meant waiting. I went in and sat with her. We didn't talk much. The next morning I set a weekly reminder: call Nu, Sunday, 8 pm. I'm Mawii, and I haven't missed one since.

Note for Naveen, left in the family diary, Sunday
Bhaijaan, you asked how Ammi is. Mostly fine. But here is what I saw this week. Every morning she dusts your room, though nobody has slept there since you left for Toronto in March. She changed the bedsheet on Friday, "in case". Twice I found her standing at your graduation photo on the landing, holding the duster, not dusting. When your call came on Wednesday she laughed at everything you said, then sat quietly on your bed for an hour.
So I've done something. I have fixed a Sunday video call, eight in the evening here, your morning. Please keep it. It isn't about news. She just needs to see your face.
Parveen
